reply.english: Sure, the fitting room is over there.
Sure, one second, let me check.

dialogue.speaker: محمود

lessons.culture: In Jeddah and Makkah, shop assistants know most customers speak different Arabic dialects or English, so they often wait for you to lead. Trying something on and saying it does not fit is completely normal and never rude. Hejazi speakers are known for their warmth and hospitality, so a shopkeeper will usually offer you tea while shopping.

exercises.prompt: A shopkeeper asks you: "إِيش مِقْيَاسَك؟" Answer that your size is large.

too_formal.feedback: This is grammatically correct, but it is a stiff, bookish way to say your clothing size.

exercises.tip: The borrowed English sizes سْمُول, مِيدْيُم, لَارْج are what people actually say in shops.

exercises.prompt: A shopkeeper asks a woman: "إِيش مِقْيَاسِك؟" Answer that your size is small.

too_formal.feedback: Understandable, but حَجْم is used for size of an object, not a person's clothing size.

exercises.tip: In Hejazi, ask a woman with مِقْيَاسِك (same as for a man).

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: "أَبِي _____ لَوْ سَمَحْت." English meaning: I want a shirt, please.

too_formal.feedback: This is a roundabout, formal way to describe a shirt; the everyday word is simply قَمِيص.

exercises.tip: أَبِي plus the item name is the everyday way to ask for something in a Hejazi shop.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: "هَذَا كَثِير _____ عَلَيّ." English meaning: This is too big for me.

too_formal.feedback: This sounds like a description of a room, not clothing that does not fit.

exercises.tip: كَثِير plus adjective plus عَلَيّ is the everyday pattern for "too X for me".

exercises.prompt: Say in Hejazi: "Can I try it on?"

too_formal.feedback: Grammatically fine but this is Modern Standard Arabic, not how it is said on the street.

exercises.tip: أَقْدَر is "can I" in everyday Hejazi speech.

exercises.prompt: Say in Hejazi: "Where's the fitting room?"

too_formal.feedback: The meaning is right but أَيْنَ and the fuller phrasing are formal; Hejazi speakers say وَيْنَ.

exercises.tip: وَيْنَ replaces أَيْنَ everywhere in Hejazi speech.

exercises.prompt: Which word means "too tight"?
exercises.tip: ضَيِّق is tight, the opposite of وَاسِع (loose/wide).

exercises.prompt: How do you ask "What's your size?"
exercises.tip: إِيش is "what" in Hejazi, and مِقْيَاس is size.

exercises.prompt: Arrange the words to say: "This is too big for me."
exercises.tip: هَذَا (this) always opens the sentence.

exercises.prompt: Arrange the words to say: "Do you have a smaller size?"
exercises.tip: عِنْدَك (do you have) opens a question about what is available.

dialogue.speaker: ليلى

dialogue.transliteration: eesh ra2yik fi hadha l-fistan l-azrag?
dialogue.english: What do you think of this blue dress?

dialogue.speaker: سَمِيرَة
dialogue.arabic: حِلْوَ كَثِير عَلَيِك، بِس فِي وَرْدِي أَحْلَى مِنْهُ.
dialogue.transliteration: hilwa katheer 3aleek, bas fi wardi a7la minuh.

dialogue.transliteration: 3indi lawn fati7 thani, daqiqa ajiibik iyyah.
dialogue.english: I have another light color, one second I'll bring it to you.

dialogue.english: Thanks, now it's nicer.

lessons.culture: Shopkeepers in Hejazi markets genuinely enjoy the back-and-forth of helping someone choose a color, often bringing out three or four options unasked. Saying a color does not suit you is heard as useful feedback, not rude. This is especially true in the souks of Jeddah and the markets around the holy mosques.

exercises.prompt: A friend asks: "إِيش رَأْيَك فِي هَذَا الْفِسْتَان؟" Say it is very nice.

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but this bookish phrasing is not how Hejazis react to a dress in a shop.

exercises.tip: حِلْوَ (nice/pretty) is the everyday word of approval for almost anything.

exercises.prompt: The shopkeeper asks: "أَيّ وَاحِد تِنْصِحُنِي فِيهِ؟" Recommend the black one and say it suits them.

too_formal.item: أَنْصَحُكِ بِاللَّوْن الْأَسْوَد لِأَنَّهُ يَلِيق بِك
too_formal.feedback: Grammatically correct, but far more formal than the quick, casual way a friend gives fashion advice.

exercises.tip: يَلِق فِيك (it suits you) is the natural compliment, dropped in casually.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: "يِعْجِبُنِي اللَّوْن _____." English meaning: I like the blue color.

too_formal.feedback: Over-specified; nobody adds "sky-blue" unless they mean a very particular shade.

exercises.tip: Colors take ال (the) when naming a specific one you like.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: "هَذَا كَثِير _____ عَلَيّ." English meaning: This is too dark for me.

too_formal.feedback: This is an exaggerated, literary way to describe a shade; غَامِق alone is what is said.

exercises.tip: غَامِق (dark) pairs with فَاتِح (light) for describing shades.

exercises.prompt: Say in Hejazi: "Do you have another color?"

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning but far too formal, like a customer-service script rather than a shop chat.

exercises.tip: ثَانِي is "other/another", used constantly in daily speech.

exercises.prompt: Say in Hejazi: "I haven't decided yet."

too_formal.feedback: Correct but stiff; لَمَّا (not yet) is the spoken word.

exercises.tip: لَمَّا مَا + verb is the everyday way to say "haven't yet".

exercises.prompt: Which word means "light" (a light color)?
exercises.tip: فَاتِح is light/pale; its opposite is غَامِق (dark).

exercises.prompt: How do you say "Just give me this one"?
exercises.tip: أَعْطِينِي (give me) is how a shopper asks to be handed an item.

exercises.prompt: Arrange the words to say: "This color doesn't suit me."
exercises.tip: مَا يْنَاسِبُنِي (doesn't suit me) comes right after naming what is wrong.

exercises.prompt: Arrange the words to say: "Which is nicer, red or blue?"
exercises.tip: وَلَّا links the two choices in an either/or question.

reply.english: It came to five thousand total.

dialogue.speaker: محمود
dialogue.english: How much is this shirt?

dialogue.english: I can't, I'll lose money at this price.

dialogue.transliteration: tayyib, thalatha w niss w khlaas.

dialogue.speaker: أَبُو عَلِي
dialogue.english: This is my final price, I swear.

dialogue.speaker: محمود

dialogue.speaker: محمود
dialogue.english: Thanks, now I'm winning too.

dialogue.speaker: أَبُو عَلِي

dialogue.english: God bless you, come again.

lessons.culture: Bargaining over clothing and textiles is expected and enjoyed in Hejazi markets and souks. A first price is almost always an opening offer, and going back and forth two or three times before agreeing is a friendly ritual, not an argument. The bargaining itself is a sign of respect—it means you value the item enough to negotiate.

exercises.prompt: You ask "إِيش سِعْرُ هَذَا؟" and the shopkeeper waits. Say it is very expensive.

too_formal.feedback: Grammatically fine but this is how a report would phrase it, not a shopper reacting out loud.

exercises.tip: غَالِي (expensive) is the blunt, everyday reaction to a high price.

exercises.prompt: You and the shopkeeper agree on a price. Say "Ok, we agreed."

too_formal.feedback: Correct but sounds like a business contract closing, not a friendly handshake over a shirt.

exercises.tip: اتِّفَقْنَا (we agreed) closes a bargain warmly and simply.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: "_____ سِعْرُ هَذَا؟" English meaning: How much is this?

too_formal.feedback: Overly wordy; the one word إِيش already means "what.".

exercises.tip: إِيش alone asks about price, quantity, or amount in Hejazi.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: "هَذَا _____ سِعْر." English meaning: This is the final price.

too_formal.item: السِّعْرُ النِّهَائِيُّ وَالْأَخِيرُ الَّذِي لَا يُمْكِنُ تَجَاوُزُهُ
too_formal.feedback: Way too elaborate; a shopkeeper just says آخِر سِعْر and means it.

exercises.tip: آخِر سِعْر (final price) is the standard way to end haggling.

exercises.prompt: Say in Hejazi: "Can you lower the price?"

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but this is how a formal request would be written, not asked across a counter.

exercises.tip: فِيك (can you) plus تِنْزِل بِالسِّعْر (lower the price) is the everyday ask.

exercises.prompt: Say in Hejazi: "Isn't there cheaper than this?"

too_formal.item: أَلَا يُوجَدُ شَيْءٌ أَرْخَصُ مِنْ هَذَا؟
too_formal.feedback: Correct but stilted; the spoken form drops straight to مَا فِي (isn't there).

exercises.tip: مَا فِي is the everyday contraction meaning "there isn't.".

exercises.prompt: Which word means "expensive"?
exercises.tip: غَالِي is expensive; its opposite is رَخِيص (cheap).

exercises.prompt: How do you say "Lower it a bit for me"?
exercises.tip: نَزِّلِي (lower for me) plus شُوَيّ (a little) softens the ask.

exercises.prompt: Arrange the words to say: "I want a discount because I'm buying a lot."
exercises.tip: لِأَنِّي (because I) links the reason to the request.

exercises.prompt: Arrange the words to say: "How much did the total come to?"
exercises.tip: صَارْ (became/came to) is used for a total reached after adding up.

dialogue.transliteration: hatman, heek ashal. min eemta shtareeteeha?

dialogue.speaker: أُمّ سَامِر
dialogue.arabic: حَتْمًا، بِتْرَجِعِك الْمَصَارِي وَلَّا بِتَبْغَيْ تَبْدِلِيهَا؟
dialogue.transliteration: hatman, btraji3ik il-masari walla bit-tabghayn tabdiliha?
dialogue.english: Sure, should I give you the money back or would you like to exchange it?

dialogue.speaker: أُمّ سَامِر

pair.english: I want to return this shirt.

response.english: What's wrong, is there a problem?
No, but I can only exchange it.

pair.english: Can I exchange it for a bigger size?

lessons.culture: Small Hejazi shops and markets usually prefer to exchange an item rather than refund cash, especially in the busy souks of Jeddah and around the holy mosques. Having the receipt makes the whole conversation much shorter and smoother. A genuine defect is almost always accepted without an argument—the shopkeeper's reputation depends on fair dealings.

exercises.prompt: The shopkeeper asks: "إِيش فِيهِ، في مُشْكِلَة؟" Say there is a defect.

too_formal.feedback: Overly technical; a customer just says فِيهِ عَيْب and points to it.

exercises.tip: فِيهِ عَيْب (there's a defect) is enough, the shopkeeper will ask to see it.

exercises.prompt: The shopkeeper asks "بِتْرَجِعْنِي مَصَارِي؟" implicitly by explaining store policy. Ask: "Can I exchange it for a bigger size?"

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but this is how a written complaint form would phrase it.

exercises.tip: فِيّ أَبْدِّلُهْ (can I exchange it) is the direct spoken ask.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: "مَعِي _____." English meaning: I have the receipt.

too_formal.feedback: Nobody in a shop calls it the "official purchase receipt"; it's just الْفَاتُورَة.

exercises.tip: الْفَاتُورَة is the everyday word for a receipt or invoice.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: "هَذَا مِقْيَاس _____." English meaning: This is the wrong size.

too_formal.item: غَيْرُ صَحِيحٍ وَلَا يَتَنَاسَبُ مَعَ الْمِقْيَاسِ الْمَطْلُوبِ
too_formal.feedback: Far too wordy; غَلَط alone means wrong here.

exercises.tip: غَلَط (wrong) is used for almost any kind of mistake in daily speech.

exercises.prompt: Say in Hejazi: "I want to return this shirt."

too_formal.feedback: Correct meaning, but this is formal phrasing, not what is said walking up to the counter.

exercises.tip: أَبِي أَرْجِع (I want to return) opens the request plainly.

exercises.prompt: Say in Hejazi: "When did you buy it?"

too_formal.feedback: Correct but stiff, sounds like a form question rather than a shopkeeper asking casually.

exercises.tip: إِمْتَى (when) is how it's asked conversationally in Hejazi.

exercises.prompt: Which word means "a defect"?
exercises.tip: عَيْب covers a flaw or defect in an object, and separately means "shameful" for behavior.

exercises.prompt: How do you say "I don't have the receipt"?
exercises.tip: مَا مَعِي (I don't have with me) negates مَعِي (I have).

exercises.prompt: Arrange the words to say: "This isn't what I ordered."
exercises.tip: الَّلِي (that which) introduces what was ordered.

exercises.prompt: Arrange the words to say: "I want to exchange it for another one."
exercises.tip: بِغَيْرَهْ (for another one of it) follows the verb أَبْدِّلُهْ (exchange it).

lessons.culture: Jeddah malls fill up after the evening prayer and stay open until around midnight, longer in Ramadan. Every mall has a مصلّى for men and one for women, and the big sales, تخفيضات, come before Eid and in the summer; prices are fixed, so people ask about a sale rather than bargain.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Where is the prayer room?"

too_formal.feedback: أين is written Arabic. Hejazi asks "where" with فين.

exercises.tip: فين (feen) is the Hejazi "where".

exercises.prompt: Translate: "I'm just looking."

too_formal.feedback: فقط is the written "only". In speech it is بس.

exercises.prompt: Which word means "floor" (storey) in a Saudi mall?
exercises.tip: الدور التاني is the second floor.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence asks where to pay?
Complete: "فين _____ الكهربائي؟" (Where is the escalator?)
exercises.tip: Many people also call it الدرج الكهربائي.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "المول متى _____؟" (When does the mall close?)

too_formal.feedback: يُغلق is what a sign says. People ask متى يقفل؟

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order: "عند / نتقابل / المدخل؟" (Shall we meet at the entrance?)
Put the words in order: "دور؟ / الجزم / في / أيّ / محلّ" (Which floor is the shoe shop on?)
exercises.tip: Hejazi often puts the thing first and the question word after it.

exercises.prompt: Your friend asks: "فين وقّفت السيّارة؟" Say in the car park downstairs.

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but nobody spells it out like that. في الموقف تحت is enough.

exercises.prompt: The shop assistant asks: "تبغى مساعدة؟" Tell him you're just looking.
exercises.tip: A woman would be asked تبغي مساعدة؟ and answers the same way.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Is there a sale in this shop?"

exercises.tip: فيه (fee) means "there is"; the question is only in the voice.

dialogue.english: Thank you very much.

lessons.culture: Saudis shop online a great deal, and الدفع عند الاستلام, paying on delivery, is still common; paying by card at the door is called دفع بالشبكة. Couriers phone before they come and often find you by the national short address, العنوان الوطني, rather than a street name.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Where is my order?"

too_formal.feedback: أين is written Arabic; Hejazi asks with فين.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Is delivery free?"

too_formal.feedback: هل is left out in speech; the rising voice makes the question.

exercises.tip: ببلاش (bi-balaash) is another everyday word for "free".

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means "Add it to the cart"?
Which word means "address"?
Complete: "أقدر أدفع عند _____؟" (Can I pay on delivery?)
exercises.tip: الدفع عند الاستلام is how Saudi shops write "cash on delivery".

exercises.prompt: Complete: "الشحنة وصلت _____." (The parcel arrived damaged.)
exercises.tip: خربان / خربانة is the everyday word for broken or damaged.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order: "بالبطاقة / أدفع / أبغى" (I want to pay by card.)
Put the words in order: "للمنتج / تقييم / حكتب" (I'll write a review of the product.)

too_formal.feedback: سـ is the written future; Hejazi uses حـ: حكتب.

exercises.prompt: Customer service asks: "إيش المشكلة؟" Say the parcel arrived damaged.

too_formal.feedback: Grammatical but written. On the phone you say الشحنة وصلت خربانة.

exercises.prompt: The seller asks: "تدفع بالبطاقة؟" Ask whether you can pay on delivery instead.

too_formal.feedback: هل يمكنني is written Arabic. In speech "can I" is أقدر.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "How much is the delivery fee?"

too_formal.feedback: رسوم is the word on the website. Speaking, people just ask التوصيل بكم؟

exercises.tip: بكم (bi-kam) asks a price.

challenge.title: A Shopping Trip in the Souk
challenge.instructions: Write and act a shopping conversation that lasts at least 10 lines. It must include asking for an item by size, discussing a color choice, checking the price, bargaining at least once, and a return or exchange with the receipt mentioned. Use at least 8 target phrases from Unit 6 and include both a masculine-address and a feminine-address form.
required_elements: An opening request using أَبِي and a clothing item.
A size question using إِيش مِقْيَاسَك or إِيش مِقْيَاسِك.
A color question or preference using اللَّوْن.
A price question using إِيش سِعْرُ.
At least one bargaining line using فِيك تِنْزِل بِالسِّعْر أو نَزِّلِي شُوَيّ.
A final price line using آخِر سِعْر.
A return or exchange line using أَبِي أَرْجِع or أَبِي أَبْدِّلُهْ.
A mention of the receipt using الْفَاتُورَة.
A closing thank-you or blessing such as يَسْلَمُو or اللَّهُ يُبَارِك فِيك.

dialogue.speaker: سَامِر
dialogue.arabic: السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكُمْ، أَبِي قَمِيص، مِقْيَاسِي لَارْج.
dialogue.english: Hello, I want a shirt, my size is large.

dialogue.speaker: أَبُو عَلِي
dialogue.arabic: وَعَلَيْكُمُ السَّلَامُ، أَهْلًا. أَيّ لَوْن تَبْغَى؟
dialogue.transliteration: wa 3alaykum assalaam, ahlan. ayy lawn tabgha?
dialogue.english: Welcome. What color do you like?

dialogue.speaker: سَامِر
dialogue.arabic: يِعْجِبُنِي اللَّوْن الْأَزْرَق. إِيش سِعْرُ هَذَا؟
dialogue.transliteration: yi3jibuni l-lawn l-azrag. eesh sir3 hadha?
dialogue.english: I like the blue color. How much is this?

dialogue.speaker: أَبُو عَلِي
dialogue.english: This is three thousand.

dialogue.speaker: سَامِر
dialogue.english: Very expensive, can you lower the price?

dialogue.speaker: أَبُو عَلِي
dialogue.arabic: نَزِّلِك لِأَلْفِين وَنِص، هَذَا آخِر سِعْر.
dialogue.transliteration: nazzilak li-alfeen w niss, hadha aakhir sir3.
dialogue.english: I'll lower it to two and a half thousand for you, this is the final price.

dialogue.speaker: سَامِر
dialogue.english: Ok, we agreed.

dialogue.speaker: ليلى
dialogue.arabic: (بَعْدَ يَوْمِينِ) السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكُمْ، أَبِي أَرْجِع هَالْقَمِيص، فِيهِ عَيْب.
dialogue.transliteration: (ba3d yawmain) assalaam 3alaykum, abi arji3 hal-gamiis, fiih 3ayb.
dialogue.english: (two days later) Hello, I want to return this shirt, there's a defect.

dialogue.speaker: أَبُو عَلِي
dialogue.english: What's wrong with it? Do you have the receipt?

dialogue.speaker: ليلى
dialogue.english: Yes, I have it. A loose thread.

dialogue.speaker: أَبُو عَلِي
dialogue.arabic: حَتْمًا، هِيك أَسْهَل. بِتَبْغَيْ تَرْجِعِيهَا وَلَّا تَبْدِلِيهَا؟
dialogue.transliteration: hatman, heek ashal. bit-tabghayn tarji3iha walla tabdiliha?
dialogue.english: Sure, that makes it easier. Do you want to return it or exchange it?

dialogue.speaker: ليلى
dialogue.arabic: أَبِي أَبْدِّلِهَا بِغَيْرِهَا، بِمِقْيَاس أَكْبَر شُوَيّ.
dialogue.transliteration: abi abdiliha bi-ghayirha, bi-migyaas akbar shwayy.
dialogue.english: I want to exchange it for another, a slightly bigger size.

dialogue.speaker: أَبُو عَلِي
dialogue.arabic: حَتْمًا، وَلَا يِهِمَّك، تَفَضَّلِي شُوفِي إِيش فِي.
dialogue.transliteration: hatman, wala yhimak, tafaddali shuufi eesh fi.
dialogue.english: Sure, don't worry, go ahead and see what's there.

dialogue.speaker: ليلى
dialogue.english: Thanks a lot, God bless you.
